definition: An idealised object that absorbs all the electromagnetic radiation falling on it and, at any given temperature, emits the most radiation that any surface can.
The total power radiated by a black body is $L = \sigma A T^{4}$, so it depends on its surface area and on the fourth power of its absolute temperature; a real surface radiates less.
The total power radiated by a body, such as a star, measured in watts or as a multiple of the Sun's luminosity.

The power received from a source per unit area at the observer, in $\text{W m}^{-2}$; for a source radiating equally in all directions, $b = \frac{L}{4\pi d^{2}}$, so it depends on distance as well as luminosity.
The power carried by radiation or a wave per unit area, through a surface at right angles to the direction of travel, in $\text{W m}^{-2}$; for a wave it is proportional to the amplitude squared.
A rule in which a quantity is proportional to $\frac{1}{d^{2}}$, the inverse of the square of the distance from a point source, so doubling the distance divides it by four.

The range of wavelengths a source emits, often shown as intensity against wavelength; a black body gives a continuous spectrum, while the atoms of a hot, low-density gas give lines at certain wavelengths only.

The peak wavelength of a black body's spectrum is inversely proportional to its absolute temperature, $\lambda_\text{max} T = 2.9 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{m K}$, so hotter bodies peak at shorter wavelengths.
